extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of classical geometry (mathematicians, historians of mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from an older Italian geometry treatise presenting propositions about pyramids, similar solids, areas and volumes, and practical measurement methods. Contains theorems about proportionality (similar pyramids/triangles), formulaic relations for lateral areas and volumes (including circular bases and spheres), and instrumented measurement instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar pyramids proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: "Icpiramg de rimili infra lo2o fonno ne la p^opoatione cubicata delatifimili." (similar pyramids are in the cubic proportion of their sides)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement and demonstration that when pyramids are similar, their corresponding linear measures are in a constant ratio and their volumes are in the cube of that ratio. The text gives algebraic/manipulative examples (placing quantities in proportion, multiplying/dividing) to show how one pyramid's volume relates to another's by the cube of the ratio of corresponding sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of similar figures scale as square of linear ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages asserting that triangles (and similar plane figures) that are similar have areas proportional to the squares of corresponding sides (e.g. various statements about "triangoli fimili" and their superfici being in proportional relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly uses similarity of triangles cut by parallels to infer area ratios (examples: triangles a b g and c ?), and applies this to faces of pyramids to relate lateral surface elements. Several worked numeric examples show multiplication/division to obtain the scaled areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel cuts produce similar cross-sections and preserve proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit and explicit statements that cutting a pyramid by a plane parallel to the base produces a smaller, similar polygonal section whose edges and areas are proportional to the original base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to derive relations between portions of pyramids (e.g., to compute areas/volumes of truncated pyramids). The author demonstrates by comparing triangles formed by apex and base edges and using proportionality of corresponding sides to get area and volume proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lateral-surface/triangle-sum multiplication relation for pyramid sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Several passages assert a relation between the altitude (cathetus) or its fractional part and the sum of areas of triangular faces when determining the area/volume of a (cut) pyramid (phrases like: "la multiplicatione de la ter^a parte dcl.t k.ne congionto dcle fuperfidc de triangoli... fa larea del tagliamento de la piramide").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses the product of a (fraction of a) perpendicular/altitude and a combination (sum) of triangular face areas to produce area/volume quantities of pyramid portions; numeric exemplifications follow. The exact algebraic form is given through worked numeric multiplications in the examples rather than a single modern formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Columnar (circular-base) pyramid surface/area relations using diameters and circumferences
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'piramide colonnare' (base a circle) the lateral surface and related measures can be obtained by multiplicative relations involving diameters, semicircumferences, arcs and certain straight lines (e.g. phrases about multiplying the diameter/half-circumference by other segments to obtain the lateral area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats circular bases separately: he relates the half-circumference (or other parts of the base circle) and chosen straight lines (medians/perpendiculars) to the lateral surface and to derived volumes, with explicit numeric computations for examples. The exposition includes instructions on choosing lines from the center to circumference and multiplying them by arc measures to get areas of the columnar pyramid's lateral surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume (corporal area) of a sphere via surface × a linear factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Passage: "larea corporale Duna fpera vuoli larea Dda fuperficie di detta fpera nel fetto Del Diametro dì Detta fpera multiplica e la multiplicatione fia larea corpora[le] predetta..." — the claim that a sphere's 'area corporale' (volume) is obtained by multiplying its surface-area by a proportion of its diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a classical assertion linking surface area and volume of a sphere via multiplication by a linear measure (the text presents it in the older language and then works numeric examples). The text proceeds through proportional decomposition of the diameter and multiplications to produce numerical factors; the demonstration style is classical/geometric (not modern symbolic calculus). (Reader should note older terminology and arithmetic examples are used rather than modern formula notation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of arc/diameter partitioning to compute portions of areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for dividing circles (e.g. dividing a circle by two diameters into quarters and then partitioning arcs into equal parts) and using proportional arc/chord relations to determine areas or parts of pyramids/circular figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed constructional steps: divide circle into four by diameters, use regolo (rule) and chords to mark equal arc segments, then use these equal arcs and their associated straight lines to perform multiplicative area computations. The text contains worked numeric examples and explicit constructional recipes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical measuring instruments and procedures (gnomo/regolo/quare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions for measuring by eye and with simple instruments: e.g. a square (quadrato) divided into 60 parts used as a rule, a 'gnomo' or graduated rod, a compass/rod for transferring measures; how to place the instrument on a plane/point and mark off parts for later multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives step-by-step practical advice on constructing and using simple measuring devices (a square divided into 60 parts, 'biaci' wedges, regolo, compassi) to estimate lengths/angles and to carry numerical proportions into area/volume computations. He emphasizes careful placement of the instrument (selecting a stable reference point) and checking for accumulated error; examples of dividing a side into parts (60, 40, etc.) illustrate measurement workflows.
